name: npm init
desc: Writes a default package.json in the current folder. The -y flag accepts every prompt, which is what you want in an exam.
example:
mkdir bookings-api
cd bookings-api

# Default manifest: name from the folder, version 1.0.0, no dependencies.
npm init -y

# Edit one field without opening an editor.
npm pkg set type=module
npm pkg set private=true

cat package.json
body:
Interactive `npm init` asks for name, version, description, entry point, test command, repository, keywords, author and license. Only name and version change behavior, and `-y` fills both from the folder name.

`npm init` does not create folders, install packages, or touch git. Those are separate commands.

name: package.json
desc: The manifest npm reads. It names the project, chooses the module system, lists commands and records installed packages.
body:
`type` is the field that decides how every `.js` file is parsed: `"module"` for `import`, anything else for `require`. `main` is only used when the package is imported as a package, not when you run `node server.js`.

The caret range `^4.21.2` accepts newer minor and patch releases but not a new major version. A trailing comma anywhere in this file stops npm with `EJSONPARSE`.

name: npm install
desc: Downloads a package into node_modules and records it in package.json. With no argument it installs everything the manifest lists.
example:
# Runtime packages: needed by the running server.
npm install express cors dotenv mysql2

# No argument: install what package.json already lists.
npm install

# See what is installed at the top level.
npm ls --depth=0
body:
Installing without a name is the normal command after cloning a repository. Installing with a name also writes the entry, so the two commands are not interchangeable.

A version suffix pins what gets recorded: `npm install express@4.21.2` writes an exact version, `npm install express@^4` writes a caret range.

name: npm install --save-dev
desc: Installs a package used only during development, so a production install can skip it.
example:
# Nodemon restarts the server while you edit. Production never runs it.
npm install --save-dev nodemon

# The short form writes the same field.
npm install -D eslint

# npm ci --omit=dev installs runtime packages only, as a deploy would.
npm ci --omit=dev
body:
Anything that only watches files, lints, or runs tests belongs in `devDependencies`. Express, cors, dotenv and mysql2 belong in `dependencies` because the server imports them at runtime.

Putting nodemon in `dependencies` still works, and it makes every deploy larger for a tool that is never started.

name: npm ci
desc: Installs exactly the versions in package-lock.json, after deleting node_modules. It fails when the manifest and lockfile disagree.
example:
# Reproduce the tested tree on a fresh clone or a build server.
npm ci

# Runtime packages only, for a deploy folder.
npm ci --omit=dev

# If it fails with a lockfile mismatch, refresh the lock and try again.
npm install
npm ci
body:
`npm install` may update the lockfile; `npm ci` never does. That difference is why a build pipeline uses `npm ci` and why the same word in the exam answer is usually worth the point.

Commit `package-lock.json`. Without it `npm ci` cannot run.

name: npm run
desc: Runs a command from the scripts object, with node_modules/.bin on PATH. Everything after -- is passed to the command.
example:
# List every script in the nearest package.json.
npm run

# Run one by name.
npm run dev

# start and test are shortcuts, no run needed.
npm start
npm test

# Flags go after -- or npm may eat them.
npm run lint -- --fix
body:
npm also understands `pre<script>` and `post<script>` hooks, so `npm run dev` can run `predev` first. Use a hook for a cheap check such as "does .env exist", not for real work.

The exit code of the command becomes npm's exit code, so a failing test fails the pipeline.

name: scripts
desc: The named commands npm can run. start and test are the two names that run without the word run.
body:
`start` must work with no arguments, because hosting platforms and markers call it by name. `check` costs one line and catches a syntax error in a second.

Names with a colon group related commands, for example `db:ping` and `db:seed`, and `npm run` lists them in one block.

name: nodemon
desc: Restarts the Node process when a watched file changes. A development tool, installed with --save-dev.
example:
# Install locally, then call it through npm so node_modules/.bin is on PATH.
npm install --save-dev nodemon

# package.json
# "dev": "nodemon server.js"
npm run dev

# Optional nodemon.json beside package.json
# {
#   "watch": ["server.js", "routes", "config"],
#   "ext": "js,json",
#   "ignore": ["node_modules"],
#   "delay": 200
# }
body:
Node 18.11 and later ship `node --watch`, which does the same job with no dependency. Use nodemon when the machine may run an older Node, and say why in a comment.

`delay` waits a moment after a save so an editor that writes a file twice does not trigger two restarts.

name: import and export
syntax:
import name from './file.js';
export default name;
desc: The ES module syntax. It needs type: module in package.json, and a relative import needs the file extension.
body:
Named and default exports coexist: `export function createApp()` is imported with braces, `export default` without. A package can be used from both module systems, but one file cannot mix `import` and `require`.

Omitting `.js` on a relative import produces `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, and the message shows the path without an extension, which reads like a typo rather than a missing rule.

name: require and module.exports
desc: The CommonJS syntax, still the default when package.json has no type field. Relative paths may omit the extension.
body:
CommonJS runs the file once and caches the exported object, so every `require` of the same path returns the same pool. ESM does the same for the module instance.

`__dirname` exists here and does not exist in ESM. When converting, add `"type": "module"`, change the syntax, and add `.js` to every relative path.

name: import.meta.url
desc: Gives the folder of the current ES module file, the ESM replacement for __dirname.
body:
`import.meta.url` is a `file://` URL, so `fileURLToPath` converts it before `path.dirname` can be used. Skipping that step produces paths such as `file:/home/user/project`, which most file APIs reject.

Avoid absolute paths built from `process.cwd()` when the file must be found next to the code, because the working directory depends on where npm was started.

name: dotenv/config
desc: Loads .env into process.env at import time. Existing shell variables win, and every value arrives as a string.
body:
The import must come before any module that reads the environment while loading, such as a connection pool created at import time. A pool built before dotenv runs sees `undefined` and falls back to defaults, which looks like a database outage.

For options use the function form: `dotenv.config({ path: '.env.local', override: true })`. `override` makes the file win over the shell.

name: process.env
desc: Reads an environment variable. Values are strings or undefined, so convert numbers and compare booleans explicitly.
body:
`process.env.PORT` is the string `"3000"`, not the number. `Number(...)` or `parseInt(..., 10)` fixes arithmetic; a `||` fallback covers the missing case.

A variable that is set to an empty string is not missing. `process.env.DB_PASSWORD || 'default'` treats both as missing, which is usually what you want for a password field.

name: .env and .env.example
desc: One key per line, no quotes needed for simple values. .env stays out of git; .env.example is committed with the same keys.
example:
# .env, local values, listed in .gitignore
PORT=3000
NODE_ENV=development
CORS_ORIGIN=http://localhost:5173
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=3306
DB_USER=root
DB_PASSWORD=
DB_NAME=bookings

# .env.example, committed, same keys, no secret values
# PORT=3000
# DB_USER=
# DB_PASSWORD=
body:
A `#` starts a comment at the start of a line or after whitespace, so a password containing `#` must be quoted. `NAME=Danube View` keeps the space; `NAME="Danube View"` drops the quotes.

Write `.gitignore` before the first commit. Removing `.env` later does not remove the password from git history.

name: cors()
desc: Lets a browser page from another origin read the API response. It is not authentication and does not stop curl.
body:
The browser blocks a cross origin read unless the response carries `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. `cors()` adds that header, and the middleware must be registered before the routes so it runs on every request including errors.

Credentials change the setup: `cors({ origin: '...', credentials: true })` plus `fetch(url, { credentials: 'include' })` on the client. A wildcard origin cannot be combined with credentials.

name: npm audit
desc: Lists known vulnerabilities in the installed tree, read from the lockfile. npm audit fix updates inside the allowed ranges.
example:
# Report only. Exit code 1 when a vulnerability is found.
npm audit

# Update packages within the existing semver ranges.
npm audit fix

# Show what a forced major upgrade would change, without doing it.
npm audit fix --dry-run --force

# Check one direct dependency and its tree.
npm ls express
body:
The report separates direct dependencies from transitive ones. A finding deep in the tree is usually fixed by updating the package that pulls it in, not by editing the lockfile by hand.

`--force` crosses major versions, so run the app and the tests afterwards. Ten minutes before a deadline is the wrong moment for it.
